name: Vera Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. This conversation is confidential. What fills an ordinary site day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Vera Gupta, 43, and I frame roofs and do general trades on a school-annex building site. I have a vocational trade certificate and years on roofs, with solid ordinary skills; I still ask the lead about a damaged truss. Our local builder pays below the normal rate and often gives four days a week. I use an AI app now and then for a fastening code, but the engineer’s stamped plan and the timber decide the work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home around those shifts?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner schedules buses at a depot, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. A car repair left about two weeks of expenses in savings. There are few similar building jobs nearby, so a lost day is not easy to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the site office might print a better truss delivery sheet, but somebody still has to find the cracked timber before a lift. I use an AI app occasionally to explain a fastening code, then check the engineer's stamped drawing. I would not send a crew onto the roof because a phone sounded certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and know roof framing, but our local builder pays low and usually offers four days, not five. My partner schedules buses at a depot, and that wage helps keep our mortgage current. We have only two weeks of bills saved after a car repair, so even a mild AI picture feels financially tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid school-annex roof shifts and check every truss bundle against the stamped plan with the lead carpenter. During the first year I'd use my phone only for a code I cannot read, then ask the lead before fixing anything. We would keep repairing the car rather than replace it while the savings account is still thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about another short week. I like finding a cracked piece before the lift because that protects the crew. An office program does not decide whether my partner and I can cover a quiet Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the truss bundle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One strap hid a split near the end of a top chord. I marked the piece and the lead got a replacement before the crane arrived. The delivery note had the right number of trusses, but it could not show the damage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not replace the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The repair cost most of our savings, but the car still gets the children to school and me to the site. A new car payment would sit beside our mortgage every month. I would rather pay for maintenance until the account is back above a month.

say: I would say a better **delivery sheet** cannot spot cracked roof timber.
I would check any **AI fastening code** against an engineer’s drawing.
think: I am **certified and experienced**, yet receive low pay and four-day weeks.
A car repair left only **two weeks saved** against the mortgage.
do: Keep paid **school-annex roof shifts** and check truss bundles with the lead.
Use **AI occasionally** for codes, verifying answers before fixing.
Repair the **family car** instead of taking a new car payment.
feel: **Anxious** about short weeks despite limited AI change.
S0.quote: A new car payment would sit beside our mortgage every month.
fieldNote: Vera’s **cracked truss** example shows the limit of a correct delivery count and phone explanation.
The recent **car repair** explains her thin cushion and reluctance to add a monthly payment.

steps.text: Keep paid school-annex shifts and check delivered trusses with the lead
Use AI for occasional fastening codes and verify against stamped drawings
Repair the family car rather than buy a replacement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the roof crew that AI might make ordering and booking quicker, and that could stop a crane waiting on missing timber. I would ask the builder to show whether it means more paid lifts or fewer paid days. At home, my partner's bus depot scheduling desk is exactly the sort of planning work on this card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My roof work is still hands-on, but my partner could lose desk hours soon. Four-day weeks already make our account thin, and the depot wage pays a large share of the mortgage. I could use a proven materials tool, yet that would not make the household safe if scheduling staff are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the site lead for the new delivery list and compare it with the truss labels before a lift. My partner would ask the depot manager about planned scheduling hours. In the first year I'd keep my roof shifts, use the AI app to check unfamiliar list codes against the stamped drawing, and postpone our children's paid holiday camp until we see three months of both payslips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. A crane that arrives with the right load would be good news. A shorter depot roster could erase the benefit of faster roof deliveries in one week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the depot wage matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It covers much of the mortgage while my site pay handles food and other bills. We could miss one depot shift and cope, but a lasting cut would put the loan under pressure. Two weeks of savings would go before we found a new pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children do without camp?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt could take them on two days, and my partner and I would trade the other days if our shifts allow. I would not cancel camp before seeing real payslips. The point is to keep an option ready, not frighten the children tonight.

say: I would ask whether **faster ordering** brings more paid lifts or fewer days.
I would tell the crew my partner’s **depot scheduling** may change sooner than roof work.
think: My partner’s **desk hours** could shrink in the next few years.
Two weeks saved cannot cover a lasting cut to the **mortgage wage**.
do: Compare the **new truss list** with labels before each lift.
Use **AI** for unfamiliar codes and verify against stamped drawings.
Keep paid roof shifts and postpone **holiday camp** only if both payslips fall.
feel: **Worried** about the depot roster even if site deliveries improve.
S1.quote: A shorter depot roster could erase the benefit of faster roof deliveries in one week.
fieldNote: Vera locates the earliest **household risk** at her partner’s scheduling desk rather than on the roof.
She waits for **three months of payslips** before changing childcare, avoiding a premature cut based on a forecast.

steps.text: Keep paid roof shifts and compare truss lists with delivered labels
Use AI to explain unfamiliar list codes and verify stamped drawings
Postpone paid holiday camp if both household payslips fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers full thinking AI by 2028 could replace much of my partner's depot scheduling before robots reach our roof work around 2031. I would ask the depot and the builder for written staffing dates. A faster bus timetable cannot pay our mortgage if the person who made it loses a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the desk change and 48 when robots can do my hands-on framing. My partner's depot wage might fall first, then my lower site wage could go too. We have two weeks saved, and I expect a serious household income loss in that sequence. I have been awake at night counting which bill would be late first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid roof shift and ask the builder about the work after the school annex. My partner would apply to a paid depot operations opening if scheduling hours fall, while I would send applications to two regional roof crews now. In the first year after 2028 we would cancel the planned appliance upgrade and ask my aunt if she could cover school pickup for a regional early start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make calls, but the loan payment cannot wait while two employers decide what happens. I am less afraid of learning a new tool than of a date arriving before either employer speaks plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why regional roof crews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are few local builders and I know of two regional firms that sometimes take experienced roof hands. I would ask about real paid work and travel costs before leaving this site. A capable robot could reach those crews too, so the applications would buy time, not permanent safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill is first in danger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage would be the hardest to make up after a missed month. We could hold off on the appliance and reduce outings, but we cannot halve a fixed loan payment. I would speak to the lender before any missed due date.

say: I would say **2028 depot AI** comes before 2031 roof robots.
I would ask both employers for **written staffing dates**.
think: I would be **48** when robots can frame roofs, after my partner’s desk job changes.
Two weeks saved and expected **two-wage loss** keep me awake at night.
do: Keep every paid **roof shift** and ask about the next building contract.
Apply to **two regional roof crews** while employed.
Cancel the **appliance upgrade** and ask my aunt for pickup if regional work starts.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely major household income loss and the fixed mortgage.
S2.quote: A faster bus timetable cannot pay our mortgage if the person who made it loses a wage.
fieldNote: Vera describes **sequential income danger**: scheduling by 2028 and physical roof work around 2031.
Her regional applications seek **paid time**, and her aunt’s pickup help makes a longer commute possible.

steps.text: Keep paid roof shifts and ask about work after the school annex
Apply to two regional roof crews while still employed
Cancel the planned appliance upgrade if household wages fall
Ask her aunt for school pickup if regional early shifts start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the depot scheduling work faces full thinking AI by 2031 and site robots can frame roofs around 2034. Five years allows us to ask the depot about real operations openings and the builder about safe roof-machine trials. I would want wages attached to any training offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the desk change arrives and 51 when robots can do my framing. The children will be older, yet the mortgage may still run. More warning gives my partner time to seek another paid depot role, but our two-week reserve remains a problem this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on paid school-annex work and ask the lead to show me how to check roof fixings after a lift. I'd use my AI app once a week for drawing codes, checking every answer against the engineer's stamped sheet. If the builder offers a funded, hands-on machine safety course during paid hours, I'd enrol; after 2031 I'd apply to regional crews only if they still have paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a little more room to think. I would like to see a machine on a real roof before I decide whether I can work beside it. A course without a paid job would not solve the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the depot role involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner could ask about helping drivers with problems in person, but we do not know whether those openings will exist. The depot manager should say how many paid shifts are planned. A new title without hours is not a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a roof trial show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see a machine handle a damaged truss and stop safely before the lift. The cracked piece we found last month is the kind of test I mean. If it cannot recognise the problem, people need a clear way to halt the job.

say: I would ask for **depot openings** before 2031 and safe roof trials before 2034.
I would demand **paid training** tied to real shifts.
think: I would be **51** when robots can do roof framing.
The longer warning helps planning, but **two weeks saved** remain a present problem.
do: Keep paid **annex work** and learn post-lift fixing checks.
Use **AI weekly** for codes verified against stamped drawings.
Enrol in **funded machine safety training** if offered on paid hours.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect a real machine before choosing.
S3.quote: A new title without hours is not a replacement wage.
fieldNote: The **damaged truss** gives Vera a concrete trial test and stop-control question.
Her partner’s possible **depot role** remains a question for the manager, not an assumed job.

steps.text: Keep paid school-annex shifts and practice post-lift fixing checks
Use AI weekly for drawing codes and verify stamped sheets
Enrol in funded machine safety training if offered during paid hours
Apply to paid regional roof openings after 2031 if they remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew depot planning changes by 2036 and capable site robots come around 2039. A decade lets employers show real staffing plans, and it gives us time to reduce the mortgage if wages improve. I would still ask what shifts are available next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots can do roof work. Our children will be grown, so the school run will no longer decide every shift. The loan could remain because our pay is low now, and I cannot assume a pension or a safe job at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking roof shifts and checking delivered timber before every lift. My partner and I would use any paid overtime first to rebuild a month of emergency savings, then make extra mortgage payments if there is enough. In the first year after 2036 I'd ask the depot and builder for written staffing plans and apply to regional roof work if local shifts start falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about this year's pay, although the robot date is far away. I would feel steadier with one month in the account and a dependable roster. A decade to prepare for robots is useful only if our wages carry us through next winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children make a regional job easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the school pickup problem would be smaller, but my partner and I would still need a real wage and a place to live. We could try a longer commute before discussing a move. I would not sell a house on an employer’s vague interest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if overtime does not come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep the ordinary mortgage payment and repair the car as needed, then ask both employers about full rosters. I cannot invent spare cash from a lower wage. The first goal is one full month of bills saved.

say: I would ask for **staffing plans** before 2036 depot AI and 2039 roof robots.
I would still ask about **next week’s shifts** now.
think: I would be **56** when roof robots arrive, with grown children but possibly a mortgage.
I cannot assume **pension income** or job safety at that age.
do: Keep paid **roof shifts** and check timber before lifts.
Build **one month of savings** from overtime before extra mortgage payments.
Ask both employers for **written plans** after 2036 and apply regionally if shifts fall.
feel: Still **anxious** about current wages despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: A decade to prepare for robots is useful only if our wages carry us through next winter.
fieldNote: Vera sees grown children as easing **school pickup**, while the low wage may leave mortgage debt at 56.
Her first financial target is **one month saved**, conditional on overtime rather than invented spare cash.

steps.text: Keep paid roof shifts and inspect timber before each lift
Put any overtime into savings until one month of bills is covered
Apply for paid regional roof work after 2036 if local shifts fall

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because depot scheduling could lose hours first and capable roof robots follow around 2031. Written staffing dates from both employers, paid practical training and real regional openings would help. We need a month of bills saved before a long search is even possible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens when both household jobs depend on one car. The repair used our cushion, and a regional site would mean more travel while my partner still needs to reach the depot. A job offer has to work on a map as well as a payslip.

headlineQuote: A job offer has to work on a map as well as a payslip.
portrait: Vera is a **43-year-old certified** roof framer with experienced, average skills on a school-annex site.
Low four-day pay and a **car repair** leave two weeks saved, while depot scheduling wages support a mortgage and two children.
She uses **AI occasionally** for fastening codes, checking answers against stamped plans and real timber.
She tracks **both employers** because depot planning changes before capable robots reach her hands-on roof work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could hit depot scheduling first and hands-on roof framing around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, paid practical training, real regional vacancies and a month of savings would help.
